binaryEX <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lewv/sp25stats21/refs/heads/main/data/binaryEX.csv")

mod1 <- glm(admit ~ gre + gpa , data = binaryEX, family = binomial)
mod2 <- glm(admit ~ gre + gpa + rank, data = binaryEX, family = binomial)

t1 <- tbl_regression(mod1, exponentiate = TRUE, digits =5)
t2 <- tbl_regression(mod2, exponentiate = TRUE, digits =5)

tbl_merge(
    tbls = list(t1, t2),
    tab_spanner = c("**Model 1**", "**Model 2**")
  )

text:
What is Shiny?

R Shiny is used for creating interactive web applications in R. Users can change what they see using Shiny.
Shiny is for others to interactively explore our data. Users do not need to know R.
Shiny can be used to analyze data and create graphics and summaries - but the point is it is typically built for others.
If your data updates, Shiny can automatically update the data. This means users always see the most current information.

title: Lecture 04 Part 2
text:
How does Shiny work?

We use R to write the code for what the Shiny app should do with the data, e.g. compute summary stats, draw graphs, etc.
We also use R to design what the app will look like.

example — where the buttons, graphs, and sliders will be placed on a screen.

The R Shiny function converts your code into a web app that can be accessed through a browser

title: Lecture 04 Part 1
text:
Background notes UI/UX

User Interface (UI) design starts with user experience (UX) research and design. Why?
Understand the target audience & what will create the best experience for it

Who will be your users (committee only? something bigger?)
What will they expect to get out of it (needs, solutions)
How will we structure their experience so they get what they need from us?

Have an idea about what is most likely to work with the target audience

title: Lecture 04 Part 1
text:
More on UX

UX then is a user-centered design philosophy, very research-like, basically studying user interfaces that work for other people.
The original example might be Nielsen, Jakob. “Enhancing the explanatory power of usability heuristics.” Proceedings of the SIGCHI conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems. 1994.
A little dated, but probably pioneered the application of factor analytic methods to address interface usability issues.
The lessons from the past could be summarized with a few guidelines derived from Usability Testing Essentials by Carol M. Barnum

title: Lecture 04 Part 1
text:
User Experience Guidelines

In spite of all the changes over the last 3-4 decades, some things do not change

People have goals
People expect to find things in certain places (expectation based on past experience, shopping carts, hamburgers, logos)
People enjoy action/movement

title: Lecture 04 Part 1
text:
Example

Amazon, YouTube, Gmail all have the following

Logo at the top-left
A search bar in the top-center
Other controls such as account/cart or settings on the top-right

Users can find their way around different sites without relearning navigation.
Familiarity breeds trust

title: Lecture 04 Part 1
text:
User Experience Design Steps

Have empathy by understanding the user through observation and/or research
Identify important user problems/issues
Develop possible solutions (brainstorm)
Build quick/draft versions of the end product in response
(ideally) Test by observing users interacting with the quick version
Repeat as needed

title: Lecture 04 Part 1
text:
Concept - Simplicity

Keep any visualizations uncluttered
Clutter is not just about having a lot on screen it is about how easily the message in the data is communicated
Elements of the graphic should contribute to the viewer’s understanding of the data
When users must pause to decode the visualization before they can think about the data, it is cluttered

title: Lecture 04 Part 1
text:
Metrics

Tufte Data-ink ratio = (ink used for data) / (total ink used in the chart)
Cleveland, etc. the human eye reads position and length best, area, color hue, and angle are more prone to errors
Gestalt principles from psychology - humans possess pattern-recognition rules (proximity, similarity, alignment) when violated the viewer’s brain must impose order (hard work).

title: Lecture 04 Part 1
text:
Simplicity - avoid unnecessary additions

Excessive decorative graphics are distracting

unnecessary background images
ornate font styles
decorative borders



if additional graphics do not offer additional information or context for your main graphic/story, consider omitting them.

title: Lecture 04 Part 1
text:
Simplicity - avoid too much data

Omit data that is not relevant to the analysis or story

Beware of confusing the audience.
If you are talking about trends over time, probably shouldn’t display individual data points (use lines instead)
The extra data will not contribute to understanding

title: Lecture 04 Part 1
text:
Simplicity - avoid overdoing color

Using too many colors or very bright colors can lead to visual confusion.
Use color to highlight significant data points
Use color to highlight important categories


Carefully cosider before using color only to make a graph colorful.

title: Lecture 04 Part 1
text:
Simplicity - avoid too many dimensions

Adding a third dimension to a visualization can complicate the interpretation.

Using a 3D chart where a 2D chart is acceptable may make it more difficult for others to interpret your chart/see your story.
Humans don’t process those kinds of images as well as they process simpler (e.g. bar chart) designs.

title: Lecture 04 Part 1
text:
Simplicity - avoid unnecessary labels

Too many labels can clutter a visualization.
Don’t need to label every single data point
Try grouping labels if labeling is unavoidable

title: Lecture 04 Part 1
text:
Concept - Balance

Idea - the elements of a graphic have different “weights” (perception)

Different graphical elements have the power to draw attention differently
Be mindful of size, color, texture, and position

title: Lecture 04 Part 1
text:
Balance - Size

Larger elements draw more attention than smaller ones
So label important information in larger fonts
Also plot important data with bigger markers

title: Lecture 04 Part 1
text:
Balance - Color

Bright colors and/or high contrast colors draw more attention than muted colors.

a bright red point on a graph will draw the eye faster than a pale blue one

Flat color backgrounds in particular, can help to create simple designs

They can reduce visual clutter and distractions which helps data points, lines, and labels to stand out.
Can unify different elements of a visualization when there are multiple types of data representations (e.g., bars, lines, and points) in the same graphic

title: Lecture 04 Part 1
text:
Balance - Complexity

Complex graphical elements in shape or texture attract more attention than simple ones.
A data point represented by a complex icon might stand out more than one represented by a simple circle.

title: Lecture 04 Part 1
text:
Balance - Position

Graphical elements placed in the center are perceived as “heavier” than those near the edges (human spatial processing.
In the US (and other left to right reading nations) graphical elements placed in the top left area can get more attention.
The opposite is true of nations where reading runs from right to left.

title: Lecture 04 Part 1
text:
Balance - Quantity

Many small graphical elements grouped together can have more visual weight than one large graphical element.
Useful for visualizations like scatter plots and heat maps.

title: Lecture 04 Part 1
text:
Concept - Alignment/Flow/Layout

It’s not just about text
All elements in a graphic should work together to create an organized appearance

This helps lead a viewer’s eye through your story/data

Strategic placement and organization of all visual elements within a graph, dashboard, or any infographic helps clarity and cohesion.

title: Lecture 04 Part 1
text:
Checklist - Alignment/Flow

Aligning text and labels for easily correlation with values
Titles and subtitles in a consistent position
Multiple graphical comparisons? - use parallel axes and uniform scales if possible

title: Lecture 04 Part 1
text:
Concept - Uniformity

To help your viewer focus on interpretation and understanding your story, you reduce the cognitive load by:
similar color schemes
consistent axes
recurring shapes or symbols


You do not want them spending time figuring out what each element represents each time they look at a visualization in your report/thesis/etc.

title: Lecture 04 Part 1
section: Always Focus on the Message first
text:
Always Focus on the Message first

Before adding additional elements:

ask if it helps communicate the core message

Watch your use of White Space

Effective use of white space can reduce clutter
Effective use of white space can focus attention on the story.

title: Lecture 04 Part 1
text:
Considerations

Design a visualization so that the most important information catches the viewer’s eye first
Then follow it with the secondary details
This can be accomplished through good use of size, color, and placement.
Keep the focus on the story that you are trying to “tell”

                margin = margin(r = base_size, unit = "pt")), 
            axis.ticks = element_line(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank(), 
            axis.title = element_text(size = rel(1)), axis.title.x = element_text(),

            legend.key = element_rect(linetype = 0), legend.key.size = unit(1.2,

            legend.text = element_text(size = rel(1.25)), legend.title = element_text(size = rel(1), 
                hjust = 0), legend.position = "top", legend.direction = NULL, 
            legend.justification = "center", panel.background = element_rect(linetype = 0),

title: Week 5, Part 2
text:
ESRI + Shapefile

ESRI (Environmental Systems Research Institute) dominates GIS software and solutions - environmental management, local government, utilities, transportation
ESRI is used for mapping, spatial analysis and also decision-making with geographic data..
The Shapefile a data format for GIS software. It is developed and regulated by ESRI it stores the location, shape, and attributes of geographic features in a map.
It is being superceded by the geopackage (gpkg)

title: Week 5, Part 2
text:
Geopackage vs Shapefile








Feature
GeoPackage (.gpkg)
Shapefile (.shp)




File Structure
Single file that can contain multiple datasets
Multiple files (.shp, .dbf, .shx, etc.) for a single dataset


Data Types
Vector, raster, and non-spatial tables
Vector data only


File Size Limit
No file size limit
2 GB maximum


Performance
Fast and efficient, especially with large files
Becomes sluggish with files over ~500 MB


Field Names
Supports full-length field names
Limited to 10 characters


Portability
Easy to share as a single file
Requires zipping and unzipping multiple files


Standard
Open, standards-based (OGC)
Primarily an Esri format specification

title: Week 5, Part 2
text:
Inside a shapefile

A shapefile is actually a folder/directory consisting of at minimum three files.
All 3 must be present for the shapefile to be complete and functional:

.shp — the file that stores the geometric location and shape of all features.
.shx — the shape index format; a positional index of the feature geometry to allow for seeking forward quickly to the geometry of a feature in the .shp file.
.dbf — an attribute table for each shape, in dBase IV (1979) format.

A choropleth map is a thematic map in which areas are shaded or patterned in proportion to the measurement of the statistical variable being displayed
Provides easy visualization of measurement variation across a geographic area

Typically darker shades often represent higher values, and lighter shades represent lower values.
The data should be standardized (adjusted for the size of the population or area).

About
Leaflet is used for creating interactive maps. Many websites use it to create maps for reporting purposes. This document serves as an brief introduction to some of its features.
The package leaflet must be installed. We call it up with the library function. It is best to use the “pipe” operator |> to pass data as the function calls can become quite complex.
The basic steps used in creating a map in leaflet:

Create a map widget by calling leaflet().
Add layers to the map by using layer functions to modify the map widget.
Repeat step 2 as many times as you like
Print the map widget to display it.

title: Week 5, Part 2

Here is a very basic map centered on the Stat Department. m is the map widget. We use addTiles() to add a base map then we use addMarkers to identify UCLA. Then we print the map.

  addTiles() |>
  addMarkers(lng = -118.442506,
             lat = 34.069649,
             popup = "UCLA")
m  # Print the map

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import math

def facet_plot(df, group_col, x, y, kind='line', figsize=(8, 4), sharex=True, sharey=False, **kwargs):
    """
    Create faceted subplots for each group in `group_col`.

    Parameters:
    - df: DataFrame
    - group_col: column to group/facet by
    - x: column for x-axis
    - y: column for y-axis
    - kind: plot type ('line', 'scatter', 'bar')
    - figsize: tuple for individual subplot size
    - sharex/sharey: whether to share axes across subplots
    - kwargs: passed to pandas plot function
    """

    groups = df[group_col].unique()
    n = len(groups)

    # Calculate grid size (e.g., 3 rows x 2 columns for 6 plots)
    cols = math.ceil(math.sqrt(n))
    rows = math.ceil(n / cols)

    fig, axs = plt.subplots(rows, cols, figsize=(figsize[0] * cols, figsize[1] * rows),
                            sharex=sharex, sharey=sharey)

    axs = axs.flatten()

    for i, group in enumerate(groups):
        ax = axs[i]
        subset = df[df[group_col] == group]

        subset.plot(kind=kind, x=x, y=y, ax=ax, legend=False, **kwargs)
        ax.set_title(f"{group_col}: {group}")
        ax.set_xlabel(x)
        ax.set_ylabel(y)

    # Hide any unused subplots
    for j in range(i + 1, len(axs)):
        fig.delaxes(axs[j])

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

import requests
import pandas as pd
pd.set_option('display.max_columns', None)

url = "https://data.wa.gov/api/odata/v4/f6w7-q2d2?$format=json"

rows = []
next_url = url  # first page

params = {
    "$top"   : "100",
    "$select": "county,make,model,model_year"
}

while next_url: # will run while this is not empty 
    print("Fetching:", next_url) # just a status indicator, where are we

    if next_url == url: # on the first pass
        r = requests.get(next_url, params=params) # apply the parameters on the first
    else:
        r = requests.get(next_url) # all other

    r.raise_for_status() # just in case we have an error
    data = r.json() # converts the response to a python object
    rows.extend(data["value"])  # make the list longer

    if "$top" in params:
        break

    next_url = data.get("@odata.nextLink") # next_url updated by what the website returns until the end

Proposed Learning Outcomes
The overall goal of this course is to provide students with the foundations necessary for understanding and building on their existing skillset with emphasis on the clear and effective visual communication of data. After this quarter, students will have:

An understanding of how to explore and analyze data to discover patterns, trends, insights and then to communicate these to a larger audience,
An understanding of data models: ways of structuring, organizing and transforming different types of data (quantitative, qualitative, spatial) for effective visualization,
An understanding of graphical perception/perceived visual information. Applying some of the cognitive principles related to visual perception and to create compelling visualizations,
The ability to use data visualization tools and supporting software, for example open-source libraries in Python (e.g., Matplotlib, Seaborn) and R (e.g., ggplot2) with , Quarto, and others,
Designing and creating interactive data visualizations that allow users to explore data at their own pace, using tools such as Streamlit (Python) or Shiny (R),

AI Assistant policy
Your instructor’s belief is AI such as Claude, ChatGPT, etc. should be used – wisely – as if it were an amazingly clever tutor or friend. But copying and pasting the code of the first example’s (below) ChatGPT response is not about learning and chances are, you will forget how to do it if you do not do it regularly. Asking ChatGPT questions in the second way gives your mind the opportunity to develop the skills scaffolding and retain the knowledge long after this course is over.






Question
Response



Please write some code in R that splits a dataset into test and training.
install.packages(“caret”) # Run only if not already installed



library(caret)



set.seed(123)



train_indices <- createDataPartition(mtcars$mpg, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)



train_data <- mtcars[train_indices, ]



test_data <- mtcars[-train_indices, ]



Let me know if you’d like to stratify the split (e.g., ensure balance on a categorical variable) or save the result to file.


Please teach me on how to write code using base R that splits a dataset into training and test with a 70-30 split - but don’t write the code for me, I want to learn how to think it through on my own.
Absolutely, I’d be glad to guide you on how to approach this! 1. Understanding the Data: - Before you begin, familiarize yourself with the dataset. Use functions like str(), head(), and summary() to understand the structure and contents of your data. 2. Setting a Seed: - To ensure that your results are reproducible, you will want to set a seed using the set.seed() function. This function controls the random number generator in R. 3. Determining the Number of Rows: - You need to know the total number of rows in your dataset to create the splits. The nrow() function can help you determine this.



4. Calculating Split Sizes: - Next, determine how many rows should go into your training and test sets. You’ll want 70% of the data to be in the training set and 30% in the test set. Use arithmetic operations to calculate the respective sizes.



5. Creating a Random Sample of Indices: - To create your training set, you’ll need to randomly select 70% of the indices (row numbers) from your dataset. You can use the sample() function to do this. Remember to use the total number of rows and the size of the training set as parameters in this function.



6. Subsetting the Dataset: - Once you have a vector of random indices, use it to subset your dataset into two parts: one for training and one for testing. In R, you can subset a data frame using square brackets []. You’ll use the vector of random indices to select rows for the training set, and the - operator to select the remaining rows for the test set.



7. Verifying Your Split: - After creating your training and test sets, verify that you’ve split the data correctly. Use the dim() function to check the dimensions of each set and ensure the split ratio is approximately 70-30. You can also use the head() function to quickly view the top rows of each set and ensure they look correct.  Remember to write your code step by step, verifying each part before moving on to the next, to avoid confusion and ensure accuracy. Once you are confident in your understanding of each step, try to write the code on your own. Good luck!

Tidying Data

Introduced the concept of melting and casting for data transformation in R
inspired similar operations in Python’s pandas library

title: Lecture 3 Part 1
text:
Wickham’s Main Points

Data reshaping — converting between “wide” and “long” formats — is essential for flexible, organized and efficient data analysis
Generally it is easier to describe the functional relationships between variables (e.g., \(weight/height^2\)) than between rows
BUT it is easier to make comparisons between groups of observations in the rows than between groups of columns.

title: Lecture 3 Part 1
text:
Wickham’s Main Points (cont’d)

Wickham writes that most datasets are not optimized for analysis. He formalizes two operations to make data more suitable for analysis:

Melting - convert wide data to long format (melt in pandas)
Casting - convert long data to wide format (pivot in pandas)

section: But why bother to do this?
text:
But why bother to do this?

Our analytic demands drive the need to tidy/reshape data
Reshaping is rearranging data without modifying values and is less aggressive than aggregating
Chances are, if you didn’t design or collect the data, the data that you are using conforms to another’s needs and not yours
Data collection methods (e.g. video, survey form) are typically disconnected from the person analyzing the data

title: Lecture 3 Part 1
section: What does it mean to tidy/reshape?
text:
What does it mean to tidy/reshape?

Change the structure of data but do not change its values

Change how data is arranged in rows and columns
Transforming wide-format data to long-format data and back again
Flattening nested data structures into 2D tabular format
Reordering dimensions in multidimensional arrays

title: Lecture 3 Part 1
text:
Tabular Data vocabulary recap

Moving between wide and Long Format

Wide implies many columns (e.g., repeated measurements), one obesrvation per row (usually)
Long implies few columns, more rows where manys row could be a single observation
Pivot implies making the rows columns, and making columns rows, usually within a table
Melt implies converting “wide” data into “long” data

title: Lecture 3 Part 1
section: Why bother? For the specific analysis.
text:
Why bother? For the specific analysis.

Random Forest, XGBoost, Logistic Regression - typically can remain “wide”
Visualization methods typically want the data to be “long”
Some deep learning methods may benefit from the data being reshaped (e.g. wide to 3D array)
EDA would probably be easier in “long” format

GIS Background

GIS stands for Geographic Information System (spatial analysis) it a framework for:

Collecting spatial data
Storing spatial data
Manipulating (cleaning, merging, transforming projections)
Analyzing (finding patterns, measuring distances, identifying clusters)
Visualizing data (creating maps) that has a place/location

title: Week 5, Part 1
text:
The sf package in R

This package has tools for geographic data operations.
It integrates with tidyverse easily (e.g., ggplot, lubridate)
Uses the “simple features” standard for storing and manipulating spatial data.
It can represent geometric objects like points, lines, polygons, and more complex objects like multipoints, multilines, and multipolygons.
See Wikipedia for more information about the simple features standard

title: Week 5, Part 1
text:
Some technical background about sf in R

An sf object is a data frame where each row represents a spatial feature (such as a geographic location or area), and each column contains the attributes associated with that feature.
One of the columns is a special list-column that contains geometry data in a format understood by the sf package
The geometries in sf objects include POINT, LINESTRING, POLYGON, MULTIPOINT, MULTILINESTRING, MULTIPOLYGON and can represent almost any kind of spatial data.
The sf package is designed work with dplyr, ggplot2, and other tidyverse packages
The sf package allows import/export to other spatial data formats,

title: Week 5, Part 1
text:
Example - Convert a data frame with point coordinates

# Convert the data frame to an sf object
points_sf <- st_as_sf(dispensary, 
                      coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), 
                      crs = 4326,
                      remove = FALSE)


st_as_sf() converts a non-spatial feature object to spatial feature
for point data, need the columns with the coordinates (x, y)
crs is the coordinate reference sysem
remove = FALSE keep the original variables

title: Week 5, Part 1
text:
What is a crs = 4326?

CRS means “Coordinate Reference System”. The CRS defines how our 2D map relates to the corresponding locations on Earth.
CRS states how the data is to be projected and how to interpret the coordinate system used in the data. It helps to align spatial data from different sources
4326 refers to a particular (there are many) CRS — WGS 84 (World Geodetic System 1984): This is the standard coordinate system used by the Global Positioning System (GPS)
Knowing which CRS matters when we bring in additional spatial information from a different source

import streamlit as st
import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px

# App title
st.title("Earthquake Explorer – SCEC 2025 Catalog")

# Load dataset
url = "https://service.scedc.caltech.edu/ftp/catalogs/SCEC_DC/2025.catalog"
column_names = ["YMD", "HMS", "ET", "GL", "MAG", "M" ,"LAT", "LON", "DEPTH", "Q",  "EVID" , "NPH", "RMS"]  

df = pd.read_csv(url, names=column_names, skiprows=10, sep=r'\s+')
df = df[:-1]  # Drop final malformed row

# Clean and process data
df['MAG'] = df['MAG'].astype(float)
df['DateTimeStr'] = df['YMD'].astype(str) + ' ' + df['HMS'].astype(str)
df['DateTime'] = pd.to_datetime(df['DateTimeStr'], format='%Y/%m/%d %H:%M:%S.%f', errors='coerce')
df = df.dropna(subset=['DateTime'])
df = df.drop(columns=['YMD', 'HMS', 'DateTimeStr'])

# Reorder and sort
cols = ['DateTime'] + [col for col in df.columns if col != 'DateTime']
df = df[cols]
df = df.sort_values('DateTime', ascending=False)

# --- Sidebar: Date Filter ---
st.sidebar.header("Filter by Date Range")
min_date = df['DateTime'].min().date()
max_date = df['DateTime'].max().date()
start_date, end_date = st.sidebar.date_input(
    label="Select range:",
    value=[min_date, max_date],
    min_value=min_date,
    max_value=max_date
)

# --- Sidebar: Magnitude Filter ---
st.sidebar.header("Filter by Magnitude")
min_mag = df['MAG'].min()
max_mag = df['MAG'].max()
mini_mag, maxi_mag = st.sidebar.slider(
    label="Select range:",
    value=[min_mag, max_mag],
    min_value=min_mag,
    max_value=max_mag
)

# Filter by date and magnitude
filtered_df = df[
    (df['DateTime'].dt.date >= start_date) & 
    (df['DateTime'].dt.date <= end_date) &
    (df['MAG'] >= mini_mag) &
    (df['MAG'] <= maxi_mag)
]

# Data Table
st.header(":blue[Earthquake Data Table] :sunglasses:")
st.dataframe(filtered_df, hide_index=True)
st.divider()

# Map Plot
map_fig = px.scatter_map(
    filtered_df,
    lat='LAT',
    lon='LON',
    color='MAG',
    size='MAG',
    hover_name='DateTime',
    zoom=6,
    height=500,
    title=f"Earthquakes from {start_date} to {end_date} with Magnitude {mini_mag}–{maxi_mag}"
)
map_fig.update_layout(mapbox_style='open-street-map')
map_fig.update_layout(margin={"r":0,"t":30,"l":0,"b":0})

st.header(":smile: :blue[Earthquake Map]")
st.subheader("using plotly and open street map", divider="gray")
st.plotly_chart(map_fig, use_container_width=True)
st.markdown("<br><br><br>", unsafe_allow_html=True)

# Depth Histogram
hist_fig = px.histogram(filtered_df, x="DEPTH")

st.header(":blue[Distribution of Depth] $d = \\frac{(v * t)}{2}$ ")
st.plotly_chart(hist_fig, use_container_width=True)
st.divider()

# Bar Plot
q_df = filtered_df['Q'].value_counts().reset_index()
q_df.columns = ['Q', 'count']
q_df = q_df.sort_values('Q')

fig = px.bar(q_df,
             x='Q',
             y='count',
             color='Q',
             title='Frequency of Quality Codes (Q)',
             labels={'Q': 'Quality Code', 'count': 'Frequency'},
             height=400)
fig.update_layout(xaxis=dict(type='category'), bargap=0.2)

st.header(":small[Quality Code Frequency where A = high]")
st.plotly_chart(fig, use_container_width=True)

If someone were to only read the label and title of your data visualization, they should still know what it was about

Avoid extra or unrelated information, what to drop is as important as what to keep.
Try outcome based story development (start with the takeaway and work backwards)
Ask others to comment/give feedback
